rows.title: Pennsylvania Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Pennsylvania Castle.
rows.summary: Pennsylvania Castle is a Gothic Revival mansion on the Isle of Portland, Dorset, England. It is located in Wakeham and overlooks Church Ope Cove.

rows.title: Castle Cornet
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Castle Cornet. Also Castle Cornet: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Cornet.
rows.summary: Castle Cornet is a large island castle in Guernsey, and former tidal island, also known as Cornet Rock or Castle Rock. Its importance was as a defence not only of the island, but of the roadstead.

rows.title: Carisbrooke Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Carisbrooke Castle. Also Carisbrooke Castle: https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1034657. Also Carisbrooke Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle.
rows.summary: Carisbrooke Castle is a historic motte-and-bailey castle located above, and to the south of, Carisbrooke village centre, on the Isle of Wight, England. Charles I was imprisoned at the castle in the months prior to his trial.

rows.title: Southsea Castle
rows.evidence: Wikidata places it on this island. Southsea Castle. Also Southsea Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southsea_Castle.
rows.summary: Southsea Castle, historically also known as Chaderton Castle, South Castle and Portsea Castle, is an artillery fort originally constructed by Henry VIII on Portsea Island, Hampshire, in 1544. It formed part of the King's Device programme to protect against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire, and defended the Solent and the eastern approach to Portsmouth.

rows.title: Oxford Castle
rows.evidence: Wikidata places it on this island. Oxford Castle. Also Oxford Castle and earlier settlement remains: https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q17650068.
rows.summary: Oxford Castle is a large, partly ruined medieval castle on the western side of central Oxford in Oxfordshire, England. Most of the original moated, wooden motte and bailey castle was replaced in stone in the late 12th or early 13th century and the castle played an important role in the conflict known as the Anarchy.

rows.title: Portland Castle
rows.evidence: Wikidata places it on this island. Portland Castle. Also Portland Castle: https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1205262. Also Portland Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Castle.
rows.summary: Portland Castle is an artillery fort constructed by Henry VIII on the Isle of Portland, Dorset, between 1539 and 1541. It formed part of the King's Device programme to protect against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire, and defended the Portland Roads anchorage.

rows.title: Elizabeth Castle
rows.evidence: the castle stands on this small island. Elizabeth Castle. Also Elizabeth Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Castle.
rows.summary: Elizabeth Castle is a castle on The Islet. Elizabeth Castle (Norman: Lé Châté Lîzabé) is a castle and tourist attraction, on a tidal island within the parish of Saint Helier, Jersey. Construction was started in the 16th century when the power of the cannon meant that the existing stronghold at Mont Orgueil was insufficient to defend the Island and the port of St Helier was vulnerable to attack by ships armed with cannons.

rows.title: Mont Orgueil Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Mont Orgueil. Also Mont Orgueil: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont_Orgueil.
rows.summary: Mont Orgueil (French pronunciation: [mɔ̃ ɔʁɡœj]; French for 'Mount Pride') is a castle in Jersey that overlooks the harbour of Gorey; a port on the east coast of the Island. It is known as Gorey Castle by English-speakers, and the "Old Castle" (lé Vièr Châté) by Jèrriais-speakers.
rows.commons_file: File:Mont Orgueil and Gorey harbour, Jersey.jpg

rows.title: West Cowes Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Cowes Castle. Also West Cowes Castle: https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1267310. Also Cowes Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowes_Castle.
rows.summary: Cowes Castle, also known as West Cowes Castle, is a Device Fort in Cowes on the Isle of Wight. Originally built by Henry VIII in 1539 to protect England against the threat of invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire, it comprised a circular bastion, flanking wings and a keep, and in 1547 it housed 17 pieces of artillery.

rows.title: Queenborough Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Queenborough Castle.
rows.summary: Queenborough Castle, also known as Sheppey Castle, is a 14th-century castle, the remnants of which are in the town of Queenborough on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent in England. The castle and the associated planned town were built on the orders of King Edward III from 1361 and named in honour his wife, Queen Philippa.

rows.title: Belvelly Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Belvelly Castle. Also Belvelly Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belvelly_Castle.
rows.summary: Belvelly Castle is a 14th or 15th-century tower house in County Cork, Ireland. It is situated next to the small village of Belvelly, opposite and overlooking the only road bridge connecting Fota Island to Great Island (on which the town of Cobh is situated).

rows.title: Ennor Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Ennor Castle.
rows.summary: Old Town (Cornish: Treveglos "church town") is a village on St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly located southeast of Hugh Town. It is thought to be the oldest settlement on the island.

rows.title: Brownsea Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Brownsea Castle. Also Brownsea Castle: https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1120277. Also Brownsea Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownsea_Castle.
rows.summary: Brownsea Castle, also known historically as Branksea Castle, was originally a Device Fort constructed by Henry VIII between 1545 and 1547 to protect Poole Harbour in Dorset, England, from the threat of French attack. Located on Brownsea Island, it comprised a stone blockhouse with a hexagonal gun platform.

rows.title: St Michael's Mount Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. St Michael's Mount. Also St Michael's Mount Castle: https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q24659597.
rows.summary: St Michael's Mount Castle is a castle on St Michael's Mount Castle. St Michael's Mount (Cornish: Karrek Loos yn Koos, meaning grey rock in the woodland) is a tidal island in Mount's Bay, near Penzance, in Cornwall, England. The island is a civil parish and is linked to the town of Marazion by a causeway of granite setts, passable (as is the beach) between mid-tide and low water.
rows.commons_file: File:St Michaels Mount in Cornwall - UK aerial image (30085819683).jpg

rows.title: Rufus Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Rufus Castle. Also Rufus Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rufus_Castle.
rows.summary: Rufus Castle is a castle on Isle of Portland. The names "Rufus Castle" and "Bow and Arrow Castle" have been widely used since the late 18th Century. It was originally speculated that Rufus referred to King William II, known as William Rufus, however more recent assessments also identify Gilbert de Clare, 7th Earl of Gloucester (the Red Earl) as a possible origin for the name.
rows.commons_file: File:Archway to Church Ope Cove - geograph.org.uk - 527904.jpg

rows.title: Sandown Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Sandown Castle, Isle of Wight.
rows.summary: Sandown Castle was a Device Fort built at Sandown on the Isle of Wight by Henry VIII in 1545 to protect against the threat of French attack. Constructed from stone with angular bastions, its design was a hybrid of Italian military architectural thinking with traditional English military design.

rows.title: Yarmouth Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Yarmouth Castle. Also Yarmouth Castle: https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1292631. Also Yarmouth Castle: https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/108538775.
rows.summary: Yarmouth Castle is an artillery fort built by Henry VIII in 1547 to protect Yarmouth Harbour on the Isle of Wight from the threat of French attack. Just under 100 feet (30 m) across, the square castle was initially equipped with 15 artillery guns and a garrison of 20 men.

rows.title: Vale Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Vale Castle, Guernsey.
rows.summary: Vale Castle, is a protected building located in the Vale, Guernsey. The original name was "Le Château St Michel", later it became "Château de Val" or "Château de Valle" and is over 1,000 years old.

rows.title: Cloghan Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Cloghan Castle (County Cork).
rows.summary: Cloghan Castle (Irish: An Clochán) is a ruined tower house on Castle Island in Lough Hyne in West Cork, Ireland. Although it no longer stands, it was originally at least three storeys tall.

rows.title: Sketrick Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Sketrick Castle. Also Sketrick Castle (ruin): https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/194295083.
rows.summary: Sketrick Castle is a castle situated on Sketrick Island near Whiterock, County Down, Northern Ireland. The castle is estimated to date back to the 12th century.

rows.title: Piel Castle
rows.evidence: Wikidata places it on this island. Piel Castle. Also Piel Castle: https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1283004. Also Piel Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piel_Castle.
rows.summary: Piel Castle, also known as Fouldry Castle or the Pile of Fouldray, is a castle situated on the south-eastern point of Piel Island, off the coast of the Furness Peninsula in north-west England. Built in the early-14th century by John Cockerham, the Abbot of neighbouring Furness Abbey, it was intended to oversee the trade through the local harbour and to protect against Scottish raids.

rows.summary: Belle Isle Castle is an 18th-century house on Belle Isle, an island previously known, in Gaelic times, as Ballymacmanus Island or Senadh-Mic-Maghnusa or, simply, Senad. The Belle Isle Estate stretches over 470-acres near Lisbellaw in County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland.

rows.title: Greeba Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Greeba Castle.

rows.title: Beaumaris Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Beaumaris Castle. Also Beaumaris Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumaris_Castle.
rows.summary: Castell Biwmares / Beaumaris Castle is a castle on Anglesey (Ynys Môn). Beaumaris Castle ( bew-MAR-is; Welsh: Castell Biwmares, Welsh pronunciation: [kastɛɬ bɪuˈmaːrɛs]), in Beaumaris, Anglesey, Wales, was built as part of Edward I's campaign to conquer north Wales after 1282. Plans were probably first made to construct the castle in 1284, but this was delayed due to lack of funds and work only began in 1295 following the Madog ap Llywelyn uprising.
rows.commons_file: File:Castell Beaumaris Castle, Ynys Mon (Anglesey), Wales 44.png

rows.title: King John's Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. King John's Castle (Limerick). Also King John's Castle (Limerick): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_John%27s_Castle_%28Limerick%29.
rows.summary: King John's Castle (Irish: Caisleán Luimnigh) also known as Limerick Castle is a 13th-century castle located on King's Island in Limerick, Ireland, next to the River Shannon. Although the site dates back to 922 when the Vikings lived on the Island, the castle itself was built on the orders of King John of England in 1200.

rows.title: Peel Castle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Peel Castle. Also Peel Castle: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peel_Castle.
rows.summary: Peel Castle (Cashtal Phurt ny h-Inshey in Manx Gaelic) is a castle in Peel in the Isle of Man, originally constructed by Norwegians. The castle stands on St Patrick's Isle, which is connected to the town by a causeway.

rows.title: Castle Rushen
rows.evidence: Wikipedia places it on this island. Castle Rushen. Also Castle Rushen: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle_Rushen.
rows.summary: Castle Rushen (Manx: Cashtal Rosien) is a medieval castle located in the Isle of Man's historic capital, Castletown, in the south of the Island. It towers over the Market Square to the south-east and the harbour to the north-east.

rows.summary: Threave Castle is a castle on Threave Island. For part of this time, the castle and the lordship of Galloway were controlled by Princess Margaret, daughter of Robert III and widow of Archibald Douglas, 4th Earl of Douglas.

rows.summary: Duart Castle, or Caisteal Dhubhairt in Scottish Gaelic, is a castle on the Isle of Mull, beside the Sound of Mull off the west coast of Scotland, within the council area of Argyll and Bute. The castle dates back to the 13th century and is the seat of Clan MacLean.

rows.title: Boat names on the cliff
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: Coast that Shaped the World places the painted boat names on the cliff at Canna pier.
rows.summary: As boats come into Canna harbour, names appear painted up the cliff behind the pier: fishing boats, their numbers, and home ports, refreshed by crews who call often. A published account of the cliff says the names are a visitors' book the boats keep themselves. One family has repainted their launch, Patrice, on visits since the 1950s.

rows.image_alt: Names painted on the cliff at Canna harbour

rows.title: Forvik declared independent
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: Reuters reported the independence declaration for the Shetland island of Forvik.
rows.summary: In June 2008 Stuart Hill declared the Shetland islet of Forvik a crown dependency and said it owed no allegiance to any United Kingdom government. Reuters reported the declaration the day it was made. Britain does not recognise the claim.
rows.image_note: Forvik, the Shetland islet in the declaration
rows.image_alt: Forvik, the Shetland islet in the declaration

rows.title: Principality of Sealand
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News places the 1967 declaration on HM Fort Roughs off Suffolk.
rows.summary: In 1967 Roy Bates declared the abandoned wartime fort HM Fort Roughs, about seven miles off Suffolk, the Principality of Sealand. Marking fifty years of the claim, the BBC described a flag, a constitution, and passports. Britain does not recognise the principality.
rows.commons_file: File:HM Fort Roughs a.k.a. Principality Of Sealand - geograph.org.uk - 1325728.jpg
rows.image_note: HM Fort Roughs, the fort called Sealand
rows.image_alt: HM Fort Roughs, the fort called Sealand

rows.title: The puffin coins
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: Time reported the 1931 coinage case in which Harman called himself sovereign of Lundy.
rows.summary: Martin Coles Harman, who bought Lundy in 1925, told the High Court in 1931 that he was sovereign of the island and entitled to issue puffin coins with his own head on them. Time reported that the court kept a fine under the Coinage Act and treated Lundy as part of the United Kingdom.

rows.title: Declared free of anthrax
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The Herald reported the 24 April 1990 declaration that Gruinard Island was safe.
rows.summary: Wartime anthrax tests left Gruinard Island closed for 48 years. On 24 April 1990 a defence minister crossed from the mainland, took down the red warning sign, and declared the island safe. The Herald reported the day.

rows.title: Fire on the anthrax island
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News, 27 March 2022, reported the fire on Gruinard Island.
rows.summary: In March 2022 a fire burned from one end of Gruinard Island to the other. The BBC reported the blaze on the uninhabited island, used for anthrax tests in the Second World War and declared clear in April 1990. The fire service said the empty island was outside its remit.

rows.title: The keepers vanished
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News places the 1900 disappearance at the Flannan Isles lighthouse on Eilean Mòr.
rows.summary: On 15 December 1900 the three keepers of the Flannan Isles lighthouse vanished from Eilean Mòr. A relief crew landed on 26 December and found the light ready, the beds empty, and the last notes from that morning. In June 2026 the BBC reported that the letter the first keeper ashore wrote would go on public display.

rows.title: A new breed of cattle
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News, 20 October 1999, places the feral herd on Swona.
rows.summary: The last residents left Swona in 1974 and the cattle stayed. In 1999 the BBC reported that the herd had bred without people for long enough to be entered as its own breed, the first new British cattle breed recognised in more than a century.

rows.title: Trainers in the post
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News, 12 September 2025, reported a parcel posted to Swona.
rows.summary: In September 2025 a parcel addressed to Swona arrived in the post: a pair of trainers, for an island whose only inhabitants are feral cattle. The BBC reported that the people who look after Swona from South Ronaldsay did not know the name on the label, and that the island has no internet from which anyone there could have ordered them.
rows.image_note: The cattle that live on Swona
rows.image_alt: The cattle that live on Swona

rows.title: Prince of the Saltees
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The Irish Times places the throne, the obelisk, and the 1953 coronation on Great Saltee.
rows.summary: Michael Neale bought Great Saltee in 1943 and styled himself Prince of the Saltees. The Irish Times records that he set a throne and an obelisk on the island, and that his coronation was held there in 1953. As a boy he had told his mother he would one day own the island and be its prince.

rows.title: The People's Republic of Eigg
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News describes the 1997 community purchase of Eigg as a declaration of a people's republic.
rows.summary: In 1997 the residents of Eigg bought their island after years of dispute with absentee landlords. A BBC account of that purchase calls it the moment a People's Republic of Eigg declared independence.

rows.image_note: Galmisdale and An Sgùrr on Eigg
rows.image_alt: Galmisdale and An Sgùrr on Eigg

rows.title: The night flight
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News places the 1975 disappearance on a night flight from Glenforsa on Mull.
rows.summary: On Christmas Eve 1975 Peter Gibbs took off alone, at night, from Glenforsa airfield on Mull and did not return. The BBC records that his body was found four months later on a hillside about a mile from the hotel, with no seawater on his clothes, and that the light aircraft was not with him.

rows.title: Castaway
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News reported the year-long Castaway settlement on Taransay.
rows.summary: In 2000 the BBC put 36 strangers on Taransay for a year and filmed them trying to build a community from scratch. By New Year seven had left, after gales that wrecked shelters they had built, a meningitis scare, and rows in public.

rows.title: Forty days on the rock
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News reports Tom McClean's 40 days living on Rockall in 1985.
rows.summary: In 1985 Tom McClean spent 40 days and nights on Rockall, living in a wooden box bolted to the rock. He told the BBC he raised a Union flag when he landed and that he was the first person to reside there. Britain had annexed the rock in 1955.

rows.title: The observatory burned
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News, 11 March 2019, reported the fire at the Fair Isle Bird Observatory.
rows.summary: On 10 March 2019 a fire destroyed the Fair Isle Bird Observatory. The BBC reported that extra crews had to be flown from Sumburgh and brought by boat, and that the smoke could be seen from the Shetland mainland. A family in the adjoining flat got out unhurt.
rows.commons_file: File:Fair Isle Bird Observatory reopened June 2010 - geograph.org.uk - 1999001.jpg
rows.image_note: The Fair Isle observatory before the 2019 fire
rows.image_alt: The Fair Isle observatory before the 2019 fire

rows.title: Crowned with beer
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News, 8 August 2025, reports the kingship attached to the Ship Inn on Piel Island.
rows.summary: Whoever takes the Ship Inn on Piel Island is crowned king or queen, and the ceremony pours a jug of beer over their head. In 2025 the BBC met the landlord, Aaron Sanderson, who said he was crowned at 33 when he took the pub. He is recorded as the island's 24th king.

rows.title: Graves in the mud
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: BBC News, 2017, places the exposed prison-hulk graves on Deadman's Island opposite Queenborough.
rows.summary: Deadman's Island, a closed mudbank in the Swale opposite Queenborough, holds unmarked graves of people who died on prison hulks more than 200 years ago. In 2017 the BBC reported that erosion was washing those coffins out of the mud. The public are not allowed on the island.
rows.commons_file: File:Dead Man's Island and Channel Marker - geograph.org.uk - 997245.jpg
rows.image_note: Deadman's Island in the Swale. Not a photograph of the graves.
rows.image_alt: Deadman's Island in the Swale. Not a photograph of the graves.

rows.title: The last feudal election
rows.licence: Summary original. Photograph via Wikimedia Commons.
rows.evidence: The Guardian, 13 December 2008, reported the election aftermath on Sark.
rows.summary: On 10 December 2008 Sark held its first fully democratic election in nearly 450 years and ended a feudal parliament. After candidates backed by the Barclay brothers lost, the Guardian reported that the brothers closed the shops, hotels, and building work they ran on the island, and that about 140 people lost their jobs.

rows.title: blonde hedgehog
rows.evidence: The source names 'blonde hedgehog' and 'Alderney'.
rows.summary: The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus), also known as the West European hedgehog, Western European hedgehog or common hedgehog, is a hedgehog species native to Europe from Iberia and Italy northwards into Scandinavia and westwards into Ireland. They are extremely rare, except on North Ronaldsay and the Channel Island of Alderney, where around 25% of the population is thought to be blonde.

rows.title: Jersey orchid
rows.evidence: The source names 'Jersey orchid' and 'Jersey'.
rows.summary: A. laxiflora is common in Normandy and Brittany (France), but in the United Kingdom it is represented only on the Channel Islands, where in Jersey it is called Jersey orchid and in Guernsey it is called Loose Flowered orchid .

rows.title: western green lizard
rows.evidence: The source names 'western green lizard' and 'Jersey'.
rows.summary: All are protected species, with Jersey being the only native habitat in the British Isles for the green lizard, wall lizard, spiny toad and agile frog.

rows.title: Guernsey vole
rows.evidence: The source names 'Guernsey vole' and 'Guernsey'.
rows.summary: The Guernsey vole (Microtus arvalis sarnius), known in Guernésiais as the mulot, is a subspecies of the common vole endemic to the island of Guernsey in the Channel Islands.

rows.title: red-billed chough
rows.evidence: The source names 'red-billed chough' and 'Isle of Man'.
rows.summary: The red-billed chough, Cornish chough or simply chough ( CHUF; Pyrrhocorax pyrrhocorax) is a bird in the crow family, one of only two species in the genus Pyrrhocorax. P. p. pyrrhocorax, the nominate subspecies and smallest form, is endemic to the British Isles, where it is restricted to Ireland, the Isle of Man, and the west of Wales, southwest Scotland, and Cornwall, which it recolonised in 2001 after an absence of 50 years.

rows.title: St Kilda dandelion
rows.evidence: The source names 'St Kilda dandelion' and 'St Kilda'.
rows.summary: Taraxacum pankhurstianum, also known as the St Kilda dandelion, is a species of dandelion that was identified as new in 2012 after being cultivated at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh from seeds collected two years previously on the island of Hirta, the largest island in the St Kilda archipelago, on the western edge of Scotland.

rows.title: St Kilda wren
rows.evidence: The source names 'St Kilda wren' and 'St Kilda'.
rows.summary: The St Kilda wren (Troglodytes troglodytes hirtensis) is a small passerine bird in the wren family. It is a distinctive subspecies of the Eurasian wren, endemic to the islands of the isolated St Kilda archipelago, in the Atlantic Ocean 64 kilometres (40 mi) west of the Outer Hebrides, Scotland.

rows.title: St Kilda field mouse
rows.evidence: The source names 'St Kilda field mouse' and 'St Kilda'.
rows.summary: The St Kilda field mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus hirtensis) is a subspecies of the wood mouse that is endemic to the Scottish archipelago of St Kilda, the island 64 kilometres (40 mi) west of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, and 160 kilometres (100 mi) from mainland Scotland.

rows.title: Fair Isle wren
rows.evidence: The source names 'Fair Isle wren' and 'Fair Isle'.
rows.summary: The Fair Isle wren (Troglodytes troglodytes fridariensis) is a small passerine bird in the wren family. It is a subspecies of the Eurasian wren endemic to Fair Isle, Shetland, Scotland, an island about halfway between mainland Shetland and Orkney.

rows.title: Shetland wren
rows.evidence: The source names 'Shetland wren' and 'Shetland'.
rows.summary: The Shetland wren (Troglodytes troglodytes zetlandicus) is a small passerine bird in the wren family. It is a subspecies of the Eurasian wren, endemic to the Shetland archipelago of Scotland, with the exception of Fair Isle which has its own endemic subspecies, the Fair Isle wren.

rows.title: Salvelinus gracillimus
rows.evidence: The source names 'Salvelinus gracillimus' and 'Shetland'.
rows.summary: Salvelinus gracillimus is a cold-water species of fish in the family Salmonidae. The species is endemic to Loch of Girlsta in the Shetland Islands; reports of specimens from Loch More on the Scottish mainland are unconfirmed.

rows.title: Orkney vole
rows.evidence: The source names 'Orkney vole' and 'Orkney'.
rows.summary: The Orkney vole (Microtus arvalis orcadensis) is a population of the common vole found in the Orkney Islands, off the northern coast of Scotland.

rows.title: Skomer vole
rows.evidence: The source names 'Skomer vole' and 'Skomer'.
rows.summary: The Skomer vole (Clethrionomys glareolus skomerensis) is a subspecies of bank vole endemic to the island of Skomer, off the west coast of Wales.

rows.title: Islay shrew
rows.evidence: The source names 'Islay shrew' and 'Islay'.
rows.summary: Sorex araneus grantii is a subspecies of the shrew Sorex araneus, found only on the Scottish island of Islay.

rows.title: Lundy cabbage
rows.evidence: The source names 'Lundy cabbage' and 'Lundy'.
rows.summary: Coincya wrightii, known as Lundy cabbage, is a species of primitive brassicoid, endemic to the island of Lundy off the southwestern coast of England, where it is sufficiently isolated to have formed its own species, with its endemic phytophagous beetles.

rows.title: Lundy cabbage flea beetle
rows.evidence: The source names 'Lundy cabbage flea beetle' and 'Lundy'.
rows.summary: Psylliodes luridipennis, commonly known as the Lundy cabbage flea beetle or the bronze Lundy cabbage flea beetle, is a species of flea beetle endemic to the island of Lundy, where it lives and feeds upon the endemic Lundy cabbage (Coincya wrightii).

rows.title: Orkney charr
rows.evidence: The source names 'Orkney charr' and 'Hoy'.
rows.summary: Salvelinus inframundus, also known as Orkney charr, is an extinct cold-water fish in the family Salmonidae which was endemic to Hoy Island, Orkney, Scotland.

rows.title: Arran service-tree
rows.evidence: The source names 'Arran service-tree' and 'Arran'.
rows.summary: Hedlundia pseudofennica, also called Arran service-tree or Arran cut-leaved whitebeam, is a species of plant in the family Rosaceae. Endemic to the Isle of Arran in Scotland, it is threatened by habitat loss.

rows.title: Arran whitebeam
rows.evidence: The source names 'Arran whitebeam' and 'Arran'.
rows.summary: Hedlundia arranensis, sometimes referred to as the Scottish or Arran whitebeam, is a species of plant in the family Rosaceae. It is endemic to the island of Arran in Scotland.

rows.title: Catacol whitebeam
rows.evidence: The source names 'Catacol whitebeam' and 'Arran'.
rows.summary: Hedlundia pseudomeinichii, known as false rowan and Catacol whitebeam, is a rare species of tree endemic to the Isle of Arran in south-western Scotland.

rows.title: Atlantic puffin
rows.evidence: The source names 'Atlantic puffin' and 'Puffin Island'.
rows.summary: Puffin Island (Irish: Oileán na gCánóg), historically called Inishfearglin, is an uninhabited steep rocky island lying off the coast of the Iveragh Peninsula, County Kerry, Ireland. Puffin Island holds important populations of several seabird species, including Atlantic puffins, Manx shearwaters and European storm-petrels, and was acquired as a nature reserve by the Irish Wildbird Conservancy (now BirdWatch Ireland) in the early 1980s.

rows.title: roseate tern
rows.evidence: The source names 'roseate tern' and 'Rockabill'.
rows.summary: The roseate tern (Sterna dougallii) is a species of tern in the family Laridae. The largest European colony, accounting for more than 75% of the European population, is in Ireland, at Rockabill Island, County Dublin.

rows.title: Shetland mouse-ear
rows.evidence: The source names 'Shetland mouse-ear' and 'Unst'.
rows.summary: Cerastium nigrescens var. nigrescens, commonly known as the Shetland mouse-ear, Shetland mouse-eared chickweed or Edmondston's chickweed, is an endemic variety of Arctic Chickweed, Cerastium nigrescens, found in Shetland, Scotland. Although reported from two other sites in the 19th century, it currently grows only on two serpentine hills on the island of Unst.

rows.title: European dark bee
rows.evidence: The source names 'European dark bee' and 'Colonsay'.
rows.summary: Colonsay and Oronsay are home to about 50 colonies of the European dark bee, Apis mellifera mellifera.

rows.title: razorbill
rows.evidence: The source names 'razorbill' and 'Handa'.
rows.summary: The breeding colonies of razorbills and guillemots on Handa are the largest in the UK, representing 11% and 9% of the total British population respectively.

rows.title: Least adder's-tongue
rows.evidence: The source names "Least adder's-tongue" and 'St Agnes'.
rows.summary: Ophioglossum lusitanicum, the least adder's-tongue, is a small fern of the family Ophioglossaceae. The distribution in Britain is restricted to one small area of coastal heath on St Agnes, Isles of Scilly where it was discovered by John Raven in 1950.

rows.title: Wild peony
rows.evidence: The source names 'Wild peony' and 'Steep Holm'.
rows.summary: Steep Holm and Flat Holm are the only known places in the UK where the wild peony has naturalised.

rows.title: Wild leek
rows.evidence: The source names 'Wild leek' and 'Flat Holm'.
rows.summary: It forms part of the City and County of Cardiff and is now managed by Cardiff Council's Flat Holm Project Team and designated as a Local Nature Reserve, Site of Special Scientific Interest and a Special Protection Area, because of the maritime grassland and rare plants such as rock sea-lavender (Limonium binervosum) and wild leek (Allium ampeloprasum).

rows.title: Red squirrel
rows.evidence: The source names 'Red squirrel' and 'Brownsea Island'.
rows.summary: The red squirrel (Sciurus vulgaris), also called Eurasian red squirrel, is a species of tree squirrel in the genus Sciurus. Brownsea Island in Poole Harbour is also populated exclusively by red rather than grey squirrels .

rows.title: European storm petrel
rows.evidence: The source names 'European storm petrel' and 'Annet'.
rows.summary: What Annet is famous for is its colonies of Manx shearwaters and storm petrels; but since they nest underground, and only come and go in the dark, there is nothing to be seen of them by day.

rows.title: Isle of Barra distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia says the Castlebay site is a gin distillery and that a whisky distillery is still being built on Barra.
rows.summary: The Isle of Barra distillery in Castlebay makes gin. A second distillery is being built on Barra so the island can start single malt whisky, which would be its first.

rows.title: Benbecula Distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia page names the distillery and Benbecula.

rows.title: Kimbland distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia page names the distillery and Sanday.

rows.title: Ardenistle distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Ardenistle Laphroaig.
rows.summary: Ardenistle was a distillery on Islay from 1837. It was later called Kildalton, then Islay, and was taken into Laphroaig in 1853.

rows.title: Ardmore (Islay)
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Ardmore (1817 Lagavulin.
rows.summary: Ardmore was a distillery on Islay from 1817 to 1835. Lagavulin took it over in 1837.

rows.title: Daill distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Daill Port Askaig Bridgend.
rows.summary: Daill was a legal distillery on Islay from 1814 to 1830. The ruins are on the road between Port Askaig and Bridgend.

rows.title: Kildalton distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Kildalton (1817 Lagavulin.
rows.summary: Kildalton was a distillery on Islay from 1817 to 1837, then merged with Lagavulin.

rows.title: Killarow distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Killarow Bridgend.
rows.summary: Killarow was a distillery on Islay from about 1760. From 1818 it was called Bridgend, and it closed in 1822. The ruins are in the village.

rows.title: Lossit distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Lossit Ballygrant.
rows.summary: Lossit, later called Ballygrant, was a distillery on Islay. It closed in 1860. The ruins are south of the village, beside the A846.

rows.title: Malt Mill
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Malt Mill Lagavulin.
rows.summary: Malt Mill was a distillery on Islay from 1908 to 1962. The site is now part of Lagavulin.

rows.title: Mulindry distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Mulindry Laggan.
rows.summary: Mulindry was a distillery on Islay in 1826 and 1827, where the Neriby Burn meets the River Laggan. It is now in ruins.

rows.title: Newton distillery (Islay)
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Newton (1819 Port Askaig Bridgend.
rows.summary: Newton was a distillery on Islay from 1819 to 1837. The ruins are beside the road between Port Askaig and Bridgend.

rows.title: Octomore distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Octomore (1816 Port Charlotte.
rows.summary: Octomore was a distillery on Islay from 1816 to 1852. The ruins are near Port Charlotte.

rows.title: Tallant distillery
rows.evidence: The Wikipedia article Islay single malts lists this closed distillery on Islay. Tallant Bowmore.
rows.summary: Tallant was a distillery on Islay from 1821 to 1852, at Tallant farm south of Bowmore.

rows.title: Islay single malts
rows.evidence: Wikipedia article Islay single malts names the protected region, the closed count, and Bowmore.
rows.summary: Islay is one of five Scotch whisky regions whose name is protected by law. The same article says as many as 23 distilleries once worked on the island, and that Bowmore in 1779 is the oldest legal distillery on record there.

rows.title: Fèis Ìle
rows.evidence: Wikipedia article Islay single malts names Fèis Ìle on Islay.
rows.summary: Islay hosts Fèis Ìle, a festival of malt and music, in the last week of May. The tastings are part of the island's whisky year.

rows.title: Portintruan distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia article Islay single malts places Portintruan between Port Ellen and Laphroaig.
rows.summary: Portintruan is a distillery being built on Islay, on the road between Port Ellen and Laphroaig. The article records that work started in 2020. It is not a working distillery yet.

rows.title: Illicit stills on Islay
rows.evidence: Wikipedia article Islay single malts places monastic distillation, smuggling, and illegal whisky production on Islay.
rows.summary: The Islay single malts article says Irish monks may have distilled on Islay in the early 1300s, and that the island's early distilleries hid in glens and caves when the excise man came. It also records home distilling, smuggling, and illegal whisky production, and says the eight older legal distilleries began as illicit stills.

rows.title: Lerwick Distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Kimbland distillery article says the Lerwick Distillery was established in Shetland in 2022. Lerwick is the port on the island recorded here as Shetland.
rows.summary: The Kimbland article says the Lerwick Distillery was established in Shetland in 2022, and that it took over the claim of most northerly Scotch whisky distillery.

rows.title: Deerness distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Kimbland distillery article places Deerness distillery in Deerness, Mainland, Orkney.
rows.summary: Deerness distillery is in Deerness on Mainland, Orkney. The Kimbland article describes it as a new Scotch whisky distillery, announced as the first on Orkney since Scapa opened in 1885, a claim Kimbland disputed.

rows.title: Manx Whiskey Company
rows.source_title: Culture of the Isle of Man
rows.evidence: The culture article states that as of 2019 the Isle of Man had a whiskey distillery run by the Manx Whiskey Company.
rows.summary: Wikipedia's article on the culture of the Isle of Man says that, as of 2019, the island had a whiskey distillery run by the Manx Whiskey Company.

rows.title: SS Politician
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's SS Politician article places the wreck, and its whisky cargo, off Eriskay.
rows.summary: SS Politician ran aground off Eriskay in 1941. Her cargo included 22,000 cases of Scotch whisky. Islanders salvaged whisky from the wreck, and Customs prosecuted them because the duty had not been paid.

rows.title: Whisky Galore!
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's article on the 1949 film says it was filmed on Barra and that the cargo was whisky.
rows.summary: Whisky Galore! is the 1949 Ealing comedy about a shipwrecked cargo of whisky. It was filmed on Barra, and the story is drawn from the grounding of the SS Politician.

rows.title: Arran's illicit stills
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Lochranza distillery article places those illegal stills on Arran.
rows.summary: The Lochranza distillery article says about fifty distilleries once stood on Arran, and that most of them were moonlight or illegal stills.

rows.title: Old Lagg distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Lochranza distillery article says the legal distillery called Lagg on Arran closed in 1837.
rows.summary: The Lochranza distillery article says a legal distillery called Lagg on Arran closed in 1837. The same article says a later distillery at Lagg, at the south end of the island, began production in 2019. This row is the closed 1837 still.

rows.title: Bunnahabhain village
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Bunnahabhain distillery article places the village, built for the workers, on Islay.
rows.summary: Bunnahabhain distillery was founded in 1881 near Port Askaig on Islay. The village of Bunnahabhain was founded to house its workers.

rows.title: Ledaig
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Tobermory distillery article says the Mull distillery was formerly Ledaig and still uses that name for its peated whisky.
rows.summary: Tobermory distillery on Mull opened in 1798 under the name Ledaig and later closed more than once. The peated whisky from the same still is still bottled as Ledaig.

rows.title: Illicit still at Highland Park
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Highland Park article places illegal distillation in 1798 on the Kirkwall site in Orkney.
rows.summary: Highland Park stands in Kirkwall on Mainland, Orkney. The article says whisky was being distilled illegally on that site in 1798, and that the distillery received a licence in 1826.

rows.title: Whisky Galore novel
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's article on the novel places the wreck it is based on off Eriskay, and Little Todday's geography on Eriskay.
rows.summary: Compton Mackenzie's novel Whisky Galore is based on the SS Politician running aground off Eriskay in 1941. The article says the cargo included 28,000 cases of malt whisky, and that Little Todday takes its geography from Eriskay.

rows.title: Whisky Galore novel
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's article on the novel says Mackenzie wrote it while living on Barra, and that Great Todday follows Barra.
rows.summary: Compton Mackenzie wrote the novel Whisky Galore while living on Barra. The article says Great Todday takes its geography from Barra.

rows.title: Loch Shiel
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Thorne Island article says the 1894 Loch Shiel wreck off the island was carrying a cargo of Scotch whisky.
rows.summary: In 1894 the sailing ship Loch Shiel ran onto rocks off Thorne Island, at the mouth of Milford Haven. The island's Wikipedia article says she was carrying Scotch whisky from Scotland to Adelaide, including cases of Glasgow whisky, and that the rescue is remembered as Wales' Whisky Galore.

rows.title: Laggan Bay distillery
rows.evidence: Ukrainian Wikipedia places Laggan Bay distillery on Islay between Bowmore and Port Ellen. Wikidata Q141284142 is a whisky distillery at 55.6838,-6.2456.
rows.summary: Laggan Bay is a malt whisky distillery on Islay, on the shore of Laggan Bay between Bowmore and Port Ellen, near the airport. The Ukrainian Wikipedia article says Ian Macleod Distillers opened it on 2 April 2026, and that it is the eleventh working distillery in the Islay region. Wikidata Q141284142 records the same still, on Islay, with no English Wikipedia article yet.

rows.title: Nun's Island Distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Nun's Island Distillery article places the Irish whiskey still on Nun's Island, Galway, and says production ceased about 1908.
rows.summary: Nun's Island Distillery made Irish whiskey on Nun's Island in Galway. The article says it was working from at least 1815, and possibly the late 1700s, until about 1908.

rows.title: Anglesey Môn distillery
rows.evidence: Wikipedia's Welsh whisky article places Anglesey Môn distillery near Pentraeth on Anglesey.
rows.summary: The Welsh whisky article lists Anglesey Môn distillery near Pentraeth on Anglesey, established in 2018, among the working whisky distilleries in Wales as of December 2022. It has no article of its own.
